newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa late starter in privatisation race.
newsitem.headline: South Africa late starter in privatisation race.

text.p: South Africa has pulled off the continent's biggest privatisation deal to date with the sale of 30 percent of Telkom for $1.26 billion, making up for a late start in the privatisation race, analysts said on Wednesday.

"South Africa has been behind the curve on privatisation. For foreign investors this deal is a very important signal because once the process starts you know there is more to come," said Constantin Vayenas, an economist at UBS in London.
"Privatisation is absolutely critical because of the capital that will flow in and because of the message it sends about the determination to trim government and open up the economy."

Sluggish progress on selling state assets has been criticised by economists who say the process is criticial to cut government borrowing, increase efficiency and demonstrate the government's commitment to market-oriented reforms.
With the Telkom deal, the process should now start to accelerate, they believe.
Posts, Telecommunications and Broadcasting Minister Jay Naidoo agreed.
"Even though we've decided each restructuring will be done on a case-by-case basis, I think we've put into place a number of very important milestones in the Telkom process," he said.
That may bring South Africa up to speed with several other African countries where reformist governments have been pushing privatisation quite aggressively.
In recent years the world's poorest continent has come round to the advantages of privatisation as a process which can inject badly-needed capital and technology.

"Coming out of their previous anti-market orientation, Africa and its leaders have rediscovered the benefits of foreign direct investment," Ken Kwaku of the World Bank told the first pan-African privatisation conference in Johannesburg earlier this month.

Zambia, arguably the continent's foremost pioneer of privatisation, moves into a critical phase this year with the sale of Zambian Consolidated Copper Mines, the mining giant which accounts for about 90 percent of export earnings.
Ghana, Kenya, Uganda, the Ivory Coast, Uganda and Mozambique are among other countries that have already taken notable privatisation steps.
The continent's economic giant, South Africa, has been slower to embrace the concept, with African National Congress politicians only recently prepared to use the "P" word.
But the mood has changed with the sale of a 30 percent stake in telecoms group Telkom to SBC Communications Inc and Telekom Malaysia Bhd.
Public Enterprises Minister Stella Sigcau said recently Pretoria had embarked on the largest and most far-reaching of restructuring of state assets on the African continent.
The World Bank's Kwaku believes privatisation can help suck in capital which has so far largely passed the continent by.
During 1995, net foreign direct investment into developing countries was about $97 billion, of which Africa received a mere $3 billion.
